title: Bidirectional BFS on New York (SoHo) ⚡
description: Visualizing Bidirectional BFS pathfinding on New York (SoHo)
ig_caption:
Bidirectional BFS: Why Meeting in the Middle Cuts Search Space in Half — how launching two simultaneous searches doubles graph traversal speed ⚡

On a real map like Amsterdam’s Jordaan, standard BFS expands outward level-by-level from the start. Bidirectional BFS instead launches BFS from BOTH ends: one queue grows from the start, the other from the goal.

Deep breakdown (the “why it’s faster” part):
• If the shortest path length is d, BFS from the start explores ~O(b^d) nodes (b = branching factor).
• Bidirectional BFS explores roughly ~O(b^(d/2)) from each side.
• Total becomes ~O(2 · b^(d/2)) ⇒ massive reduction in the number of visited nodes.

How to code it (core mechanics):
1) Maintain two frontiers/queues: qF (forward) and qB (backward).
2) Keep two visited maps: visitedF and visitedB with parent pointers for path reconstruction.
3) Expand the smaller frontier each step (practical optimization).
4) Stop as soon as a node appears in both visited sets—YOU’VE FOUND THE MEETING POINT.
5) Stitch the path: forward parents → meeting node → backward parents.

Takeaway: You don’t just “search faster”—you reduce the exponential blow-up by splitting the distance in half.

Debate question: Would bidirectional BFS always be faster on a grid graph, or can overhead/uneven branching flip the outcome?
